entry.title: [Marten] Marten's LINQ provider has SQL injection via unescaped string literals
entry.content:
Several code paths in Marten's LINQ provider and tenant-management internals interpolated a runtime, potentially attacker-influenced value into generated SQL as a single-quoted string literal without escaping or parameterization. A value containing a single quote (') could break out of the literal and inject arbitrary SQL.

The primary vector is a Dictionary<,> indexer key used in a Where filter — Where(x => x.Attributes[key] == v) — a common "filter by attribute name" / EAV pattern. It is confirmed with an executed proof-of-concept and yields filter / multi-tenant authorization bypass (returning other tenants' rows) and blind data exfiltration. Where the application permits ;-batched statements (Npgsql default), data modification is also possible.

Affected sinks

  • Linq/Members/Dictionaries/DictionaryItemMember.cs — dictionary indexer key (primary, confirmed PoC)
  • Linq/Members/Dictionaries/DictionaryContainsKeyFilter.cs — Dictionary.ContainsKey(key) (Newtonsoft serializer only; System.Text.Json escapes the quote)
  • Linq/Parsing/SelectParser.cs — a constant string projected through Select(x => new { L = runtimeString })
  • Internal/Operations/DeleteAllForTenant.cs — tenant id reaching per-tenant projection teardown via IEventStore.DeleteProjectionProgressAsync (an in-code comment wrongly claimed the value was validated)
  • Schema/DatabaseScopedTenantPartitions.cs — tenant id inlined into FOR VALUES IN ('...') partition DDL
  • Events/Daemon/Internals/EventLoader.cs (defense-in-depth) — per-tenant partition-pruning literal

Proof of concept (primary vector)

Benign: x.Attributes["nonexistent-key"] == "v" returns 0 rows. Attack: x.Attributes["nonexistent' = '' or 1=1 --"] == "v" returns all rows. Generated SQL:

select d.data from public.mt_doc_doc as d where d.data -> 'Attributes' ->> 'x' or 1=1 --' = :p0;

Fix

Each sink now escapes embedded single quotes (.Replace("'", "''"), mirroring the existing Ordering.BuildNgramRankExpression) or binds the value as a parameter (DeleteAllForTenant). Where a literal is retained for partition pruning, escaping preserves plan-time pruning while closing the injection. Regression tests lock down each vector.

Workarounds

Until upgrading: do not pass untrusted input as a dictionary indexer key / ContainsKey argument / Select constant, nor as a tenant id into projection teardown or provisioning; and disable multi-statement command batching to limit blast radius.

Credit

Reported privately and responsibly by an external security researcher with an executed PoC. Additional sinks found during the follow-up LINQ-wide audit.

References

  • https://github.com/JasperFx/marten/security/advisories/GHSA-rfx3-98h7-v3xp
  • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-75513
  • https://github.com/JasperFx/marten/pull/4911
  • https://github.com/JasperFx/marten/commit/61882d0424854cb48703f08bdb246894ac576bed
  • https://github.com/JasperFx/marten/releases/tag/9.13.0
  • https://github.com/JasperFx/marten/releases/tag/8.37.4
  • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-rfx3-98h7-v3xp

entry.title: [Magick.NET-Q16-AnyCPU] Duplicate Advisory: ImageMagick: Malicious PCD files trigger 1‑byte heap Out-of-bounds Read and DoS
entry.content:
Duplicate Advisory

This advisory has been withdrawn because it is a duplicate of GHSA-wgxp-q8xq-wpp9. This link is maintained to preserve external references.

Original Description

ImageMagick before 7.1.2-15 (and 6.x before 6.9.13-40) contains a heap out-of-bounds read in the PCD coder's DecodeImage loop. A crafted PCD file can trigger a one-byte heap out-of-bounds read during image decoding, resulting in denial of service and potential disclosure of an adjacent heap byte.

References

  • https://github.com/ImageMagick/ImageMagick/security/advisories/GHSA-wgxp-q8xq-wpp9
  • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-56378
  • https://www.vulncheck.com/advisories/imagemagick-heap-out-of-bounds-read-in-pcd-decoder
  • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-jmqv-2mx7-544h

entry.title: [Magick.NET-Q8-x86] Duplicate Advisory: ImageMagick: Integer Overflow in PSB (PSD v2) RLE decoding path causes heap Out of Bounds reads for 32-bit builds
entry.content:
Duplicate Advisory

This advisory has been withdrawn because it is a duplicate of GHSA-273h-m46v-96q4. This link is maintained to preserve external references.

Original Description

ImageMagick before 7.1.2-15 and 6.9.x before 6.9.13-40 contains an integer overflow in the PSB (PSD v2) RLE decoding path (ReadPSDChannelRLE in coders/psd.c) that causes a heap out-of-bounds read on 32-bit builds. Processing a crafted PSB file can lead to information disclosure or a crash.

References

  • https://github.com/ImageMagick/ImageMagick/security/advisories/GHSA-273h-m46v-96q4
  • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-56367
  • https://www.vulncheck.com/advisories/imagemagick-heap-out-of-bounds-read-in-psb-rle-decoding
  • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-rg39-4fm5-hrp2

entry.title: [Microsoft.NETCore.App.Runtime.win-x86] Microsoft Security Advisory CVE-2026-111497 - .NET Brotli Decoder Out-of-bounds Write Vulnerability
entry.content:
Executive summary

A buffer overflow vulnerability exists in the Brotli decompression library used by .NET. This vulnerability may allow an unauthenticated attacker to read or corrupt process memory. This could lead to information disclosure, denial of service, or elevation of privilege.

ASP.NET Core and HttpClient do not automatically decompress Brotli data in their default configurations. Applications are exposed when they enable Brotli decompression or explicitly use Brotli decompression APIs to process attacker-controlled data, as described below. .NET Framework is not affected.

Announcement

Announcement for this issue can be found at https://github.com/dotnet/announcements/issues/494

CVSS Details

  • Version: 3.1
  • Severity: High
  • Score: 8.1
  • Vector: CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:H/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H/E:U/RL:O/RC:C
  • Weakness: CWE-787 (Out-of-bounds Write)

Affected Platforms

  • Platforms: All
  • Architectures: All

Mitigations

ASP.NET Core request decompression and HttpClient automatic response decompression are not enabled by default. An application is not exposed merely because an affected .NET package is installed. Exposure requires the application to decompress attacker-controlled Brotli data through one of these paths:

  • Enable ASP.NET Core automatic request decompression with Brotli (br) support.
  • Enable HttpClient automatic response decompression by configuring HttpClientHandler.AutomaticDecompression or SocketsHttpHandler.AutomaticDecompression to include DecompressionMethods.Brotli or DecompressionMethods.All.
  • Explicitly use Brotli decompression APIs in System.IO.Compression, such as BrotliStream or BrotliDecoder.

Until the update can be deployed, avoid decompressing attacker-controlled Brotli data.

The following examples show how to disable Brotli decompression if you are already using it.

Warning: Do not use these code snippets if you are not already using decompression. Do not introduce a call to AddRequestDecompression if your application does not already call it. Similarly, do not introduce an AutomaticDecompression property assignment if your application does not already set that property. Modify only your existing decompression configuration. Enabling automatic decompression can introduce denial-of-service risks even when Brotli is excluded.

If you are already using Brotli request decompression in ASP.NET Core, exclude it by removing the br entry from your existing decompression configuration. This retains the default gzip and deflate providers:

builder.Services.AddRequestDecompression(options =>
{
    options.DecompressionProviders.Remove("br");
});

If your application already enables HttpClient automatic response decompression, disable Brotli by updating the flags on your existing handler so they do not include DecompressionMethods.Brotli:

var handler = new HttpClientHandler
{
    AutomaticDecompression = DecompressionMethods.GZip | DecompressionMethods.Deflate
};

var httpClient = new HttpClient(handler);

Applications that directly use Brotli decompression APIs must stop passing untrusted Brotli data to those APIs until updated. Ensure that other application code does not continue to decompress the same untrusted Brotli data. These changes can affect normal request and response handling and should be tested before deployment. Installing the security update remains the recommended fix.

Affected Packages

The vulnerability affects .NET applications using an affected Brotli decoder in the runtime or NativeAOT packages listed below.

Advisory FAQ

How do I know if I am affected?

You are affected if your application uses an affected Brotli decoder included in a package listed in affected packages, including a decoder linked into a NativeAOT application, to decompress attacker-controlled data. See mitigations for the affected usage paths and default settings.

How do I fix the issue?

Install the updated runtime or SDK for the .NET version used by your application. If your application directly references an affected package, update that reference to the patched version listed above.

.NET release Runtime SDK versions
.NET 8 8.0.33 8.0.133, 8.0.427
.NET 9 9.0.22 9.0.123, 9.0.320
.NET 10 10.0.14 10.0.114, 10.0.403
.NET 11 previews 11.0.0-rc.3.26522.148 11.0.100-rc.3.26522.148

Download .NET from https://dotnet.microsoft.com/download/dotnet.

Once you have installed the updated runtime or SDK, restart your apps for the update to take effect.

If you have deployed self-contained applications, rebuild and redeploy those applications with the updated runtime.

For NativeAOT applications, update the SDK and any explicit compiler or runtime-pack references to patched versions, then republish and redeploy the application. Updating the machine's shared runtime alone does not replace a decoder already linked into a NativeAOT executable.

Other Information

Reporting Security Issues

If you have found a potential security issue in a supported version of .NET, please report it to the Microsoft Security Response Center (MSRC) via the MSRC Researcher Portal. Further information can be found in the MSRC Report an Issue FAQ.

Security reports made through MSRC may qualify for the Microsoft .NET Bounty. Details of the Microsoft .NET Bounty Program including terms and conditions are at https://aka.ms/corebounty.

Support

You can ask questions about this issue on GitHub in the .NET GitHub organization. The main repos are located at https://github.com/dotnet/runtime. The Announcements repo (https://github.com/dotnet/Announcements) will contain this bulletin as an issue and will include a link to a discussion issue. You can ask questions in the linked discussion issue.

entry.title: [Microsoft.NETCore.App.Runtime.win-x64] Microsoft Security Advisory CVE-2026-111497 - .NET Brotli Decoder Out-of-bounds Write Vulnerability
entry.content:
Executive summary

A buffer overflow vulnerability exists in the Brotli decompression library used by .NET. This vulnerability may allow an unauthenticated attacker to read or corrupt process memory. This could lead to information disclosure, denial of service, or elevation of privilege.

ASP.NET Core and HttpClient do not automatically decompress Brotli data in their default configurations. Applications are exposed when they enable Brotli decompression or explicitly use Brotli decompression APIs to process attacker-controlled data, as described below. .NET Framework is not affected.

Announcement

Announcement for this issue can be found at https://github.com/dotnet/announcements/issues/494

CVSS Details

  • Version: 3.1
  • Severity: High
  • Score: 8.1
  • Vector: CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:H/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H/E:U/RL:O/RC:C
  • Weakness: CWE-787 (Out-of-bounds Write)

Affected Platforms

  • Platforms: All
  • Architectures: All

Mitigations

ASP.NET Core request decompression and HttpClient automatic response decompression are not enabled by default. An application is not exposed merely because an affected .NET package is installed. Exposure requires the application to decompress attacker-controlled Brotli data through one of these paths:

  • Enable ASP.NET Core automatic request decompression with Brotli (br) support.
  • Enable HttpClient automatic response decompression by configuring HttpClientHandler.AutomaticDecompression or SocketsHttpHandler.AutomaticDecompression to include DecompressionMethods.Brotli or DecompressionMethods.All.
  • Explicitly use Brotli decompression APIs in System.IO.Compression, such as BrotliStream or BrotliDecoder.

Until the update can be deployed, avoid decompressing attacker-controlled Brotli data.

The following examples show how to disable Brotli decompression if you are already using it.

Warning: Do not use these code snippets if you are not already using decompression. Do not introduce a call to AddRequestDecompression if your application does not already call it. Similarly, do not introduce an AutomaticDecompression property assignment if your application does not already set that property. Modify only your existing decompression configuration. Enabling automatic decompression can introduce denial-of-service risks even when Brotli is excluded.

If you are already using Brotli request decompression in ASP.NET Core, exclude it by removing the br entry from your existing decompression configuration. This retains the default gzip and deflate providers:

builder.Services.AddRequestDecompression(options =>
{
    options.DecompressionProviders.Remove("br");
});

If your application already enables HttpClient automatic response decompression, disable Brotli by updating the flags on your existing handler so they do not include DecompressionMethods.Brotli:

var handler = new HttpClientHandler
{
    AutomaticDecompression = DecompressionMethods.GZip | DecompressionMethods.Deflate
};

var httpClient = new HttpClient(handler);

Applications that directly use Brotli decompression APIs must stop passing untrusted Brotli data to those APIs until updated. Ensure that other application code does not continue to decompress the same untrusted Brotli data. These changes can affect normal request and response handling and should be tested before deployment. Installing the security update remains the recommended fix.

Affected Packages

The vulnerability affects .NET applications using an affected Brotli decoder in the runtime or NativeAOT packages listed below.

Advisory FAQ

How do I know if I am affected?

You are affected if your application uses an affected Brotli decoder included in a package listed in affected packages, including a decoder linked into a NativeAOT application, to decompress attacker-controlled data. See mitigations for the affected usage paths and default settings.

How do I fix the issue?

Install the updated runtime or SDK for the .NET version used by your application. If your application directly references an affected package, update that reference to the patched version listed above.

.NET release Runtime SDK versions
.NET 8 8.0.33 8.0.133, 8.0.427
.NET 9 9.0.22 9.0.123, 9.0.320
.NET 10 10.0.14 10.0.114, 10.0.403
.NET 11 previews 11.0.0-rc.3.26522.148 11.0.100-rc.3.26522.148

Download .NET from https://dotnet.microsoft.com/download/dotnet.

Once you have installed the updated runtime or SDK, restart your apps for the update to take effect.

If you have deployed self-contained applications, rebuild and redeploy those applications with the updated runtime.

For NativeAOT applications, update the SDK and any explicit compiler or runtime-pack references to patched versions, then republish and redeploy the application. Updating the machine's shared runtime alone does not replace a decoder already linked into a NativeAOT executable.

Other Information

Reporting Security Issues

If you have found a potential security issue in a supported version of .NET, please report it to the Microsoft Security Response Center (MSRC) via the MSRC Researcher Portal. Further information can be found in the MSRC Report an Issue FAQ.

Security reports made through MSRC may qualify for the Microsoft .NET Bounty. Details of the Microsoft .NET Bounty Program including terms and conditions are at https://aka.ms/corebounty.

Support

You can ask questions about this issue on GitHub in the .NET GitHub organization. The main repos are located at https://github.com/dotnet/runtime. The Announcements repo (https://github.com/dotnet/Announcements) will contain this bulletin as an issue and will include a link to a discussion issue. You can ask questions in the linked discussion issue.

entry.title: [Microsoft.NETCore.App.Runtime.win-arm64] Microsoft Security Advisory CVE-2026-111497 - .NET Brotli Decoder Out-of-bounds Write Vulnerability
entry.content:
Executive summary

A buffer overflow vulnerability exists in the Brotli decompression library used by .NET. This vulnerability may allow an unauthenticated attacker to read or corrupt process memory. This could lead to information disclosure, denial of service, or elevation of privilege.

ASP.NET Core and HttpClient do not automatically decompress Brotli data in their default configurations. Applications are exposed when they enable Brotli decompression or explicitly use Brotli decompression APIs to process attacker-controlled data, as described below. .NET Framework is not affected.

Announcement

Announcement for this issue can be found at https://github.com/dotnet/announcements/issues/494

CVSS Details

  • Version: 3.1
  • Severity: High
  • Score: 8.1
  • Vector: CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:H/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H/E:U/RL:O/RC:C
  • Weakness: CWE-787 (Out-of-bounds Write)

Affected Platforms

  • Platforms: All
  • Architectures: All

Mitigations

ASP.NET Core request decompression and HttpClient automatic response decompression are not enabled by default. An application is not exposed merely because an affected .NET package is installed. Exposure requires the application to decompress attacker-controlled Brotli data through one of these paths:

  • Enable ASP.NET Core automatic request decompression with Brotli (br) support.
  • Enable HttpClient automatic response decompression by configuring HttpClientHandler.AutomaticDecompression or SocketsHttpHandler.AutomaticDecompression to include DecompressionMethods.Brotli or DecompressionMethods.All.
  • Explicitly use Brotli decompression APIs in System.IO.Compression, such as BrotliStream or BrotliDecoder.

Until the update can be deployed, avoid decompressing attacker-controlled Brotli data.

The following examples show how to disable Brotli decompression if you are already using it.

Warning: Do not use these code snippets if you are not already using decompression. Do not introduce a call to AddRequestDecompression if your application does not already call it. Similarly, do not introduce an AutomaticDecompression property assignment if your application does not already set that property. Modify only your existing decompression configuration. Enabling automatic decompression can introduce denial-of-service risks even when Brotli is excluded.

If you are already using Brotli request decompression in ASP.NET Core, exclude it by removing the br entry from your existing decompression configuration. This retains the default gzip and deflate providers:

builder.Services.AddRequestDecompression(options =>
{
    options.DecompressionProviders.Remove("br");
});

If your application already enables HttpClient automatic response decompression, disable Brotli by updating the flags on your existing handler so they do not include DecompressionMethods.Brotli:

var handler = new HttpClientHandler
{
    AutomaticDecompression = DecompressionMethods.GZip | DecompressionMethods.Deflate
};

var httpClient = new HttpClient(handler);

Applications that directly use Brotli decompression APIs must stop passing untrusted Brotli data to those APIs until updated. Ensure that other application code does not continue to decompress the same untrusted Brotli data. These changes can affect normal request and response handling and should be tested before deployment. Installing the security update remains the recommended fix.

Affected Packages

The vulnerability affects .NET applications using an affected Brotli decoder in the runtime or NativeAOT packages listed below.

Advisory FAQ

How do I know if I am affected?

You are affected if your application uses an affected Brotli decoder included in a package listed in affected packages, including a decoder linked into a NativeAOT application, to decompress attacker-controlled data. See mitigations for the affected usage paths and default settings.

How do I fix the issue?

Install the updated runtime or SDK for the .NET version used by your application. If your application directly references an affected package, update that reference to the patched version listed above.

.NET release Runtime SDK versions
.NET 8 8.0.33 8.0.133, 8.0.427
.NET 9 9.0.22 9.0.123, 9.0.320
.NET 10 10.0.14 10.0.114, 10.0.403
.NET 11 previews 11.0.0-rc.3.26522.148 11.0.100-rc.3.26522.148

Download .NET from https://dotnet.microsoft.com/download/dotnet.

Once you have installed the updated runtime or SDK, restart your apps for the update to take effect.

If you have deployed self-contained applications, rebuild and redeploy those applications with the updated runtime.

For NativeAOT applications, update the SDK and any explicit compiler or runtime-pack references to patched versions, then republish and redeploy the application. Updating the machine's shared runtime alone does not replace a decoder already linked into a NativeAOT executable.

Other Information

Reporting Security Issues

If you have found a potential security issue in a supported version of .NET, please report it to the Microsoft Security Response Center (MSRC) via the MSRC Researcher Portal. Further information can be found in the MSRC Report an Issue FAQ.

Security reports made through MSRC may qualify for the Microsoft .NET Bounty. Details of the Microsoft .NET Bounty Program including terms and conditions are at https://aka.ms/corebounty.

Support

You can ask questions about this issue on GitHub in the .NET GitHub organization. The main repos are located at https://github.com/dotnet/runtime. The Announcements repo (https://github.com/dotnet/Announcements) will contain this bulletin as an issue and will include a link to a discussion issue. You can ask questions in the linked discussion issue.

entry.title: [Microsoft.NETCore.App.Runtime.tvossimulator-x64] Microsoft Security Advisory CVE-2026-111497 - .NET Brotli Decoder Out-of-bounds Write Vulnerability
entry.content:
Executive summary

A buffer overflow vulnerability exists in the Brotli decompression library used by .NET. This vulnerability may allow an unauthenticated attacker to read or corrupt process memory. This could lead to information disclosure, denial of service, or elevation of privilege.

ASP.NET Core and HttpClient do not automatically decompress Brotli data in their default configurations. Applications are exposed when they enable Brotli decompression or explicitly use Brotli decompression APIs to process attacker-controlled data, as described below. .NET Framework is not affected.

Announcement

Announcement for this issue can be found at https://github.com/dotnet/announcements/issues/494

CVSS Details

  • Version: 3.1
  • Severity: High
  • Score: 8.1
  • Vector: CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:H/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H/E:U/RL:O/RC:C
  • Weakness: CWE-787 (Out-of-bounds Write)

Affected Platforms

  • Platforms: All
  • Architectures: All

Mitigations

ASP.NET Core request decompression and HttpClient automatic response decompression are not enabled by default. An application is not exposed merely because an affected .NET package is installed. Exposure requires the application to decompress attacker-controlled Brotli data through one of these paths:

  • Enable ASP.NET Core automatic request decompression with Brotli (br) support.
  • Enable HttpClient automatic response decompression by configuring HttpClientHandler.AutomaticDecompression or SocketsHttpHandler.AutomaticDecompression to include DecompressionMethods.Brotli or DecompressionMethods.All.
  • Explicitly use Brotli decompression APIs in System.IO.Compression, such as BrotliStream or BrotliDecoder.

Until the update can be deployed, avoid decompressing attacker-controlled Brotli data.

The following examples show how to disable Brotli decompression if you are already using it.

Warning: Do not use these code snippets if you are not already using decompression. Do not introduce a call to AddRequestDecompression if your application does not already call it. Similarly, do not introduce an AutomaticDecompression property assignment if your application does not already set that property. Modify only your existing decompression configuration. Enabling automatic decompression can introduce denial-of-service risks even when Brotli is excluded.

If you are already using Brotli request decompression in ASP.NET Core, exclude it by removing the br entry from your existing decompression configuration. This retains the default gzip and deflate providers:

builder.Services.AddRequestDecompression(options =>
{
    options.DecompressionProviders.Remove("br");
});

If your application already enables HttpClient automatic response decompression, disable Brotli by updating the flags on your existing handler so they do not include DecompressionMethods.Brotli:

var handler = new HttpClientHandler
{
    AutomaticDecompression = DecompressionMethods.GZip | DecompressionMethods.Deflate
};

var httpClient = new HttpClient(handler);

Applications that directly use Brotli decompression APIs must stop passing untrusted Brotli data to those APIs until updated. Ensure that other application code does not continue to decompress the same untrusted Brotli data. These changes can affect normal request and response handling and should be tested before deployment. Installing the security update remains the recommended fix.

Affected Packages

The vulnerability affects .NET applications using an affected Brotli decoder in the runtime or NativeAOT packages listed below.

Advisory FAQ

How do I know if I am affected?

You are affected if your application uses an affected Brotli decoder included in a package listed in affected packages, including a decoder linked into a NativeAOT application, to decompress attacker-controlled data. See mitigations for the affected usage paths and default settings.

How do I fix the issue?

Install the updated runtime or SDK for the .NET version used by your application. If your application directly references an affected package, update that reference to the patched version listed above.

.NET release Runtime SDK versions
.NET 8 8.0.33 8.0.133, 8.0.427
.NET 9 9.0.22 9.0.123, 9.0.320
.NET 10 10.0.14 10.0.114, 10.0.403
.NET 11 previews 11.0.0-rc.3.26522.148 11.0.100-rc.3.26522.148

Download .NET from https://dotnet.microsoft.com/download/dotnet.

Once you have installed the updated runtime or SDK, restart your apps for the update to take effect.

If you have deployed self-contained applications, rebuild and redeploy those applications with the updated runtime.

For NativeAOT applications, update the SDK and any explicit compiler or runtime-pack references to patched versions, then republish and redeploy the application. Updating the machine's shared runtime alone does not replace a decoder already linked into a NativeAOT executable.

Other Information

Reporting Security Issues

If you have found a potential security issue in a supported version of .NET, please report it to the Microsoft Security Response Center (MSRC) via the MSRC Researcher Portal. Further information can be found in the MSRC Report an Issue FAQ.

Security reports made through MSRC may qualify for the Microsoft .NET Bounty. Details of the Microsoft .NET Bounty Program including terms and conditions are at https://aka.ms/corebounty.

Support

You can ask questions about this issue on GitHub in the .NET GitHub organization. The main repos are located at https://github.com/dotnet/runtime. The Announcements repo (https://github.com/dotnet/Announcements) will contain this bulletin as an issue and will include a link to a discussion issue. You can ask questions in the linked discussion issue.

entry.title: [Microsoft.NETCore.App.Runtime.tvossimulator-arm64] Microsoft Security Advisory CVE-2026-111497 - .NET Brotli Decoder Out-of-bounds Write Vulnerability
entry.content:
Executive summary

A buffer overflow vulnerability exists in the Brotli decompression library used by .NET. This vulnerability may allow an unauthenticated attacker to read or corrupt process memory. This could lead to information disclosure, denial of service, or elevation of privilege.

ASP.NET Core and HttpClient do not automatically decompress Brotli data in their default configurations. Applications are exposed when they enable Brotli decompression or explicitly use Brotli decompression APIs to process attacker-controlled data, as described below. .NET Framework is not affected.

Announcement

Announcement for this issue can be found at https://github.com/dotnet/announcements/issues/494

CVSS Details

  • Version: 3.1
  • Severity: High
  • Score: 8.1
  • Vector: CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:H/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H/E:U/RL:O/RC:C
  • Weakness: CWE-787 (Out-of-bounds Write)

Affected Platforms

  • Platforms: All
  • Architectures: All

Mitigations

ASP.NET Core request decompression and HttpClient automatic response decompression are not enabled by default. An application is not exposed merely because an affected .NET package is installed. Exposure requires the application to decompress attacker-controlled Brotli data through one of these paths:

  • Enable ASP.NET Core automatic request decompression with Brotli (br) support.
  • Enable HttpClient automatic response decompression by configuring HttpClientHandler.AutomaticDecompression or SocketsHttpHandler.AutomaticDecompression to include DecompressionMethods.Brotli or DecompressionMethods.All.
  • Explicitly use Brotli decompression APIs in System.IO.Compression, such as BrotliStream or BrotliDecoder.

Until the update can be deployed, avoid decompressing attacker-controlled Brotli data.

The following examples show how to disable Brotli decompression if you are already using it.

Warning: Do not use these code snippets if you are not already using decompression. Do not introduce a call to AddRequestDecompression if your application does not already call it. Similarly, do not introduce an AutomaticDecompression property assignment if your application does not already set that property. Modify only your existing decompression configuration. Enabling automatic decompression can introduce denial-of-service risks even when Brotli is excluded.

If you are already using Brotli request decompression in ASP.NET Core, exclude it by removing the br entry from your existing decompression configuration. This retains the default gzip and deflate providers:

builder.Services.AddRequestDecompression(options =>
{
    options.DecompressionProviders.Remove("br");
});

If your application already enables HttpClient automatic response decompression, disable Brotli by updating the flags on your existing handler so they do not include DecompressionMethods.Brotli:

var handler = new HttpClientHandler
{
    AutomaticDecompression = DecompressionMethods.GZip | DecompressionMethods.Deflate
};

var httpClient = new HttpClient(handler);

Applications that directly use Brotli decompression APIs must stop passing untrusted Brotli data to those APIs until updated. Ensure that other application code does not continue to decompress the same untrusted Brotli data. These changes can affect normal request and response handling and should be tested before deployment. Installing the security update remains the recommended fix.

Affected Packages

The vulnerability affects .NET applications using an affected Brotli decoder in the runtime or NativeAOT packages listed below.

Advisory FAQ

How do I know if I am affected?

You are affected if your application uses an affected Brotli decoder included in a package listed in affected packages, including a decoder linked into a NativeAOT application, to decompress attacker-controlled data. See mitigations for the affected usage paths and default settings.

How do I fix the issue?

Install the updated runtime or SDK for the .NET version used by your application. If your application directly references an affected package, update that reference to the patched version listed above.

.NET release Runtime SDK versions
.NET 8 8.0.33 8.0.133, 8.0.427
.NET 9 9.0.22 9.0.123, 9.0.320
.NET 10 10.0.14 10.0.114, 10.0.403
.NET 11 previews 11.0.0-rc.3.26522.148 11.0.100-rc.3.26522.148

Download .NET from https://dotnet.microsoft.com/download/dotnet.

Once you have installed the updated runtime or SDK, restart your apps for the update to take effect.

If you have deployed self-contained applications, rebuild and redeploy those applications with the updated runtime.

For NativeAOT applications, update the SDK and any explicit compiler or runtime-pack references to patched versions, then republish and redeploy the application. Updating the machine's shared runtime alone does not replace a decoder already linked into a NativeAOT executable.

Other Information

Reporting Security Issues

If you have found a potential security issue in a supported version of .NET, please report it to the Microsoft Security Response Center (MSRC) via the MSRC Researcher Portal. Further information can be found in the MSRC Report an Issue FAQ.

Security reports made through MSRC may qualify for the Microsoft .NET Bounty. Details of the Microsoft .NET Bounty Program including terms and conditions are at https://aka.ms/corebounty.

Support

You can ask questions about this issue on GitHub in the .NET GitHub organization. The main repos are located at https://github.com/dotnet/runtime. The Announcements repo (https://github.com/dotnet/Announcements) will contain this bulletin as an issue and will include a link to a discussion issue. You can ask questions in the linked discussion issue.

entry.title: [Microsoft.NETCore.App.Runtime.tvos-arm64] Microsoft Security Advisory CVE-2026-111497 - .NET Brotli Decoder Out-of-bounds Write Vulnerability
entry.content:
Executive summary

A buffer overflow vulnerability exists in the Brotli decompression library used by .NET. This vulnerability may allow an unauthenticated attacker to read or corrupt process memory. This could lead to information disclosure, denial of service, or elevation of privilege.

ASP.NET Core and HttpClient do not automatically decompress Brotli data in their default configurations. Applications are exposed when they enable Brotli decompression or explicitly use Brotli decompression APIs to process attacker-controlled data, as described below. .NET Framework is not affected.

Announcement

Announcement for this issue can be found at https://github.com/dotnet/announcements/issues/494

CVSS Details

  • Version: 3.1
  • Severity: High
  • Score: 8.1
  • Vector: CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:H/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H/E:U/RL:O/RC:C
  • Weakness: CWE-787 (Out-of-bounds Write)

Affected Platforms

  • Platforms: All
  • Architectures: All

Mitigations

ASP.NET Core request decompression and HttpClient automatic response decompression are not enabled by default. An application is not exposed merely because an affected .NET package is installed. Exposure requires the application to decompress attacker-controlled Brotli data through one of these paths:

  • Enable ASP.NET Core automatic request decompression with Brotli (br) support.
  • Enable HttpClient automatic response decompression by configuring HttpClientHandler.AutomaticDecompression or SocketsHttpHandler.AutomaticDecompression to include DecompressionMethods.Brotli or DecompressionMethods.All.
  • Explicitly use Brotli decompression APIs in System.IO.Compression, such as BrotliStream or BrotliDecoder.

Until the update can be deployed, avoid decompressing attacker-controlled Brotli data.

The following examples show how to disable Brotli decompression if you are already using it.

Warning: Do not use these code snippets if you are not already using decompression. Do not introduce a call to AddRequestDecompression if your application does not already call it. Similarly, do not introduce an AutomaticDecompression property assignment if your application does not already set that property. Modify only your existing decompression configuration. Enabling automatic decompression can introduce denial-of-service risks even when Brotli is excluded.

If you are already using Brotli request decompression in ASP.NET Core, exclude it by removing the br entry from your existing decompression configuration. This retains the default gzip and deflate providers:

builder.Services.AddRequestDecompression(options =>
{
    options.DecompressionProviders.Remove("br");
});

If your application already enables HttpClient automatic response decompression, disable Brotli by updating the flags on your existing handler so they do not include DecompressionMethods.Brotli:

var handler = new HttpClientHandler
{
    AutomaticDecompression = DecompressionMethods.GZip | DecompressionMethods.Deflate
};

var httpClient = new HttpClient(handler);

Applications that directly use Brotli decompression APIs must stop passing untrusted Brotli data to those APIs until updated. Ensure that other application code does not continue to decompress the same untrusted Brotli data. These changes can affect normal request and response handling and should be tested before deployment. Installing the security update remains the recommended fix.

Affected Packages

The vulnerability affects .NET applications using an affected Brotli decoder in the runtime or NativeAOT packages listed below.

Advisory FAQ

How do I know if I am affected?

You are affected if your application uses an affected Brotli decoder included in a package listed in affected packages, including a decoder linked into a NativeAOT application, to decompress attacker-controlled data. See mitigations for the affected usage paths and default settings.

How do I fix the issue?

Install the updated runtime or SDK for the .NET version used by your application. If your application directly references an affected package, update that reference to the patched version listed above.

.NET release Runtime SDK versions
.NET 8 8.0.33 8.0.133, 8.0.427
.NET 9 9.0.22 9.0.123, 9.0.320
.NET 10 10.0.14 10.0.114, 10.0.403
.NET 11 previews 11.0.0-rc.3.26522.148 11.0.100-rc.3.26522.148

Download .NET from https://dotnet.microsoft.com/download/dotnet.

Once you have installed the updated runtime or SDK, restart your apps for the update to take effect.

If you have deployed self-contained applications, rebuild and redeploy those applications with the updated runtime.

For NativeAOT applications, update the SDK and any explicit compiler or runtime-pack references to patched versions, then republish and redeploy the application. Updating the machine's shared runtime alone does not replace a decoder already linked into a NativeAOT executable.

Other Information

Reporting Security Issues

If you have found a potential security issue in a supported version of .NET, please report it to the Microsoft Security Response Center (MSRC) via the MSRC Researcher Portal. Further information can be found in the MSRC Report an Issue FAQ.

Security reports made through MSRC may qualify for the Microsoft .NET Bounty. Details of the Microsoft .NET Bounty Program including terms and conditions are at https://aka.ms/corebounty.

Support

You can ask questions about this issue on GitHub in the .NET GitHub organization. The main repos are located at https://github.com/dotnet/runtime. The Announcements repo (https://github.com/dotnet/Announcements) will contain this bulletin as an issue and will include a link to a discussion issue. You can ask questions in the linked discussion issue.

entry.title: [Microsoft.NETCore.App.Runtime.osx-x64] Microsoft Security Advisory CVE-2026-111497 - .NET Brotli Decoder Out-of-bounds Write Vulnerability
entry.content:
Executive summary

A buffer overflow vulnerability exists in the Brotli decompression library used by .NET. This vulnerability may allow an unauthenticated attacker to read or corrupt process memory. This could lead to information disclosure, denial of service, or elevation of privilege.

ASP.NET Core and HttpClient do not automatically decompress Brotli data in their default configurations. Applications are exposed when they enable Brotli decompression or explicitly use Brotli decompression APIs to process attacker-controlled data, as described below. .NET Framework is not affected.

Announcement

Announcement for this issue can be found at https://github.com/dotnet/announcements/issues/494

CVSS Details

  • Version: 3.1
  • Severity: High
  • Score: 8.1
  • Vector: CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:H/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H/E:U/RL:O/RC:C
  • Weakness: CWE-787 (Out-of-bounds Write)

Affected Platforms

  • Platforms: All
  • Architectures: All

Mitigations

ASP.NET Core request decompression and HttpClient automatic response decompression are not enabled by default. An application is not exposed merely because an affected .NET package is installed. Exposure requires the application to decompress attacker-controlled Brotli data through one of these paths:

  • Enable ASP.NET Core automatic request decompression with Brotli (br) support.
  • Enable HttpClient automatic response decompression by configuring HttpClientHandler.AutomaticDecompression or SocketsHttpHandler.AutomaticDecompression to include DecompressionMethods.Brotli or DecompressionMethods.All.
  • Explicitly use Brotli decompression APIs in System.IO.Compression, such as BrotliStream or BrotliDecoder.

Until the update can be deployed, avoid decompressing attacker-controlled Brotli data.

The following examples show how to disable Brotli decompression if you are already using it.

Warning: Do not use these code snippets if you are not already using decompression. Do not introduce a call to AddRequestDecompression if your application does not already call it. Similarly, do not introduce an AutomaticDecompression property assignment if your application does not already set that property. Modify only your existing decompression configuration. Enabling automatic decompression can introduce denial-of-service risks even when Brotli is excluded.

If you are already using Brotli request decompression in ASP.NET Core, exclude it by removing the br entry from your existing decompression configuration. This retains the default gzip and deflate providers:

builder.Services.AddRequestDecompression(options =>
{
    options.DecompressionProviders.Remove("br");
});

If your application already enables HttpClient automatic response decompression, disable Brotli by updating the flags on your existing handler so they do not include DecompressionMethods.Brotli:

var handler = new HttpClientHandler
{
    AutomaticDecompression = DecompressionMethods.GZip | DecompressionMethods.Deflate
};

var httpClient = new HttpClient(handler);

Applications that directly use Brotli decompression APIs must stop passing untrusted Brotli data to those APIs until updated. Ensure that other application code does not continue to decompress the same untrusted Brotli data. These changes can affect normal request and response handling and should be tested before deployment. Installing the security update remains the recommended fix.

Affected Packages

The vulnerability affects .NET applications using an affected Brotli decoder in the runtime or NativeAOT packages listed below.

Advisory FAQ

How do I know if I am affected?

You are affected if your application uses an affected Brotli decoder included in a package listed in affected packages, including a decoder linked into a NativeAOT application, to decompress attacker-controlled data. See mitigations for the affected usage paths and default settings.

How do I fix the issue?

Install the updated runtime or SDK for the .NET version used by your application. If your application directly references an affected package, update that reference to the patched version listed above.

.NET release Runtime SDK versions
.NET 8 8.0.33 8.0.133, 8.0.427
.NET 9 9.0.22 9.0.123, 9.0.320
.NET 10 10.0.14 10.0.114, 10.0.403
.NET 11 previews 11.0.0-rc.3.26522.148 11.0.100-rc.3.26522.148

Download .NET from https://dotnet.microsoft.com/download/dotnet.

Once you have installed the updated runtime or SDK, restart your apps for the update to take effect.

If you have deployed self-contained applications, rebuild and redeploy those applications with the updated runtime.

For NativeAOT applications, update the SDK and any explicit compiler or runtime-pack references to patched versions, then republish and redeploy the application. Updating the machine's shared runtime alone does not replace a decoder already linked into a NativeAOT executable.

Other Information

Reporting Security Issues

If you have found a potential security issue in a supported version of .NET, please report it to the Microsoft Security Response Center (MSRC) via the MSRC Researcher Portal. Further information can be found in the MSRC Report an Issue FAQ.

Security reports made through MSRC may qualify for the Microsoft .NET Bounty. Details of the Microsoft .NET Bounty Program including terms and conditions are at https://aka.ms/corebounty.

Support

You can ask questions about this issue on GitHub in the .NET GitHub organization. The main repos are located at https://github.com/dotnet/runtime. The Announcements repo (https://github.com/dotnet/Announcements) will contain this bulletin as an issue and will include a link to a discussion issue. You can ask questions in the linked discussion issue.

entry.title: [Microsoft.NETCore.App.Runtime.osx-arm64] Microsoft Security Advisory CVE-2026-111497 - .NET Brotli Decoder Out-of-bounds Write Vulnerability
entry.content:
Executive summary

A buffer overflow vulnerability exists in the Brotli decompression library used by .NET. This vulnerability may allow an unauthenticated attacker to read or corrupt process memory. This could lead to information disclosure, denial of service, or elevation of privilege.

ASP.NET Core and HttpClient do not automatically decompress Brotli data in their default configurations. Applications are exposed when they enable Brotli decompression or explicitly use Brotli decompression APIs to process attacker-controlled data, as described below. .NET Framework is not affected.

Announcement

Announcement for this issue can be found at https://github.com/dotnet/announcements/issues/494

CVSS Details

  • Version: 3.1
  • Severity: High
  • Score: 8.1
  • Vector: CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:H/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H/E:U/RL:O/RC:C
  • Weakness: CWE-787 (Out-of-bounds Write)

Affected Platforms

  • Platforms: All
  • Architectures: All

Mitigations

ASP.NET Core request decompression and HttpClient automatic response decompression are not enabled by default. An application is not exposed merely because an affected .NET package is installed. Exposure requires the application to decompress attacker-controlled Brotli data through one of these paths:

  • Enable ASP.NET Core automatic request decompression with Brotli (br) support.
  • Enable HttpClient automatic response decompression by configuring HttpClientHandler.AutomaticDecompression or SocketsHttpHandler.AutomaticDecompression to include DecompressionMethods.Brotli or DecompressionMethods.All.
  • Explicitly use Brotli decompression APIs in System.IO.Compression, such as BrotliStream or BrotliDecoder.

Until the update can be deployed, avoid decompressing attacker-controlled Brotli data.

The following examples show how to disable Brotli decompression if you are already using it.

Warning: Do not use these code snippets if you are not already using decompression. Do not introduce a call to AddRequestDecompression if your application does not already call it. Similarly, do not introduce an AutomaticDecompression property assignment if your application does not already set that property. Modify only your existing decompression configuration. Enabling automatic decompression can introduce denial-of-service risks even when Brotli is excluded.

If you are already using Brotli request decompression in ASP.NET Core, exclude it by removing the br entry from your existing decompression configuration. This retains the default gzip and deflate providers:

builder.Services.AddRequestDecompression(options =>
{
    options.DecompressionProviders.Remove("br");
});

If your application already enables HttpClient automatic response decompression, disable Brotli by updating the flags on your existing handler so they do not include DecompressionMethods.Brotli:

var handler = new HttpClientHandler
{
    AutomaticDecompression = DecompressionMethods.GZip | DecompressionMethods.Deflate
};

var httpClient = new HttpClient(handler);

Applications that directly use Brotli decompression APIs must stop passing untrusted Brotli data to those APIs until updated. Ensure that other application code does not continue to decompress the same untrusted Brotli data. These changes can affect normal request and response handling and should be tested before deployment. Installing the security update remains the recommended fix.

Affected Packages

The vulnerability affects .NET applications using an affected Brotli decoder in the runtime or NativeAOT packages listed below.

Advisory FAQ

How do I know if I am affected?

You are affected if your application uses an affected Brotli decoder included in a package listed in affected packages, including a decoder linked into a NativeAOT application, to decompress attacker-controlled data. See mitigations for the affected usage paths and default settings.

How do I fix the issue?

Install the updated runtime or SDK for the .NET version used by your application. If your application directly references an affected package, update that reference to the patched version listed above.

.NET release Runtime SDK versions
.NET 8 8.0.33 8.0.133, 8.0.427
.NET 9 9.0.22 9.0.123, 9.0.320
.NET 10 10.0.14 10.0.114, 10.0.403
.NET 11 previews 11.0.0-rc.3.26522.148 11.0.100-rc.3.26522.148

Download .NET from https://dotnet.microsoft.com/download/dotnet.

Once you have installed the updated runtime or SDK, restart your apps for the update to take effect.

If you have deployed self-contained applications, rebuild and redeploy those applications with the updated runtime.

For NativeAOT applications, update the SDK and any explicit compiler or runtime-pack references to patched versions, then republish and redeploy the application. Updating the machine's shared runtime alone does not replace a decoder already linked into a NativeAOT executable.

Other Information

Reporting Security Issues

If you have found a potential security issue in a supported version of .NET, please report it to the Microsoft Security Response Center (MSRC) via the MSRC Researcher Portal. Further information can be found in the MSRC Report an Issue FAQ.

Security reports made through MSRC may qualify for the Microsoft .NET Bounty. Details of the Microsoft .NET Bounty Program including terms and conditions are at https://aka.ms/corebounty.

Support

You can ask questions about this issue on GitHub in the .NET GitHub organization. The main repos are located at https://github.com/dotnet/runtime. The Announcements repo (https://github.com/dotnet/Announcements) will contain this bulletin as an issue and will include a link to a discussion issue. You can ask questions in the linked discussion issue.

entry.title: [Microsoft.NETCore.App.Runtime.maccatalyst-x64] Microsoft Security Advisory CVE-2026-111497 - .NET Brotli Decoder Out-of-bounds Write Vulnerability
entry.content:
Executive summary

A buffer overflow vulnerability exists in the Brotli decompression library used by .NET. This vulnerability may allow an unauthenticated attacker to read or corrupt process memory. This could lead to information disclosure, denial of service, or elevation of privilege.

ASP.NET Core and HttpClient do not automatically decompress Brotli data in their default configurations. Applications are exposed when they enable Brotli decompression or explicitly use Brotli decompression APIs to process attacker-controlled data, as described below. .NET Framework is not affected.

Announcement

Announcement for this issue can be found at https://github.com/dotnet/announcements/issues/494

CVSS Details

  • Version: 3.1
  • Severity: High
  • Score: 8.1
  • Vector: CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:H/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H/E:U/RL:O/RC:C
  • Weakness: CWE-787 (Out-of-bounds Write)

Affected Platforms

  • Platforms: All
  • Architectures: All

Mitigations

ASP.NET Core request decompression and HttpClient automatic response decompression are not enabled by default. An application is not exposed merely because an affected .NET package is installed. Exposure requires the application to decompress attacker-controlled Brotli data through one of these paths:

  • Enable ASP.NET Core automatic request decompression with Brotli (br) support.
  • Enable HttpClient automatic response decompression by configuring HttpClientHandler.AutomaticDecompression or SocketsHttpHandler.AutomaticDecompression to include DecompressionMethods.Brotli or DecompressionMethods.All.
  • Explicitly use Brotli decompression APIs in System.IO.Compression, such as BrotliStream or BrotliDecoder.

Until the update can be deployed, avoid decompressing attacker-controlled Brotli data.

The following examples show how to disable Brotli decompression if you are already using it.

Warning: Do not use these code snippets if you are not already using decompression. Do not introduce a call to AddRequestDecompression if your application does not already call it. Similarly, do not introduce an AutomaticDecompression property assignment if your application does not already set that property. Modify only your existing decompression configuration. Enabling automatic decompression can introduce denial-of-service risks even when Brotli is excluded.

If you are already using Brotli request decompression in ASP.NET Core, exclude it by removing the br entry from your existing decompression configuration. This retains the default gzip and deflate providers:

builder.Services.AddRequestDecompression(options =>
{
    options.DecompressionProviders.Remove("br");
});

If your application already enables HttpClient automatic response decompression, disable Brotli by updating the flags on your existing handler so they do not include DecompressionMethods.Brotli:

var handler = new HttpClientHandler
{
    AutomaticDecompression = DecompressionMethods.GZip | DecompressionMethods.Deflate
};

var httpClient = new HttpClient(handler);

Applications that directly use Brotli decompression APIs must stop passing untrusted Brotli data to those APIs until updated. Ensure that other application code does not continue to decompress the same untrusted Brotli data. These changes can affect normal request and response handling and should be tested before deployment. Installing the security update remains the recommended fix.

Affected Packages

The vulnerability affects .NET applications using an affected Brotli decoder in the runtime or NativeAOT packages listed below.

Advisory FAQ

How do I know if I am affected?

You are affected if your application uses an affected Brotli decoder included in a package listed in affected packages, including a decoder linked into a NativeAOT application, to decompress attacker-controlled data. See mitigations for the affected usage paths and default settings.

How do I fix the issue?

Install the updated runtime or SDK for the .NET version used by your application. If your application directly references an affected package, update that reference to the patched version listed above.

.NET release Runtime SDK versions
.NET 8 8.0.33 8.0.133, 8.0.427
.NET 9 9.0.22 9.0.123, 9.0.320
.NET 10 10.0.14 10.0.114, 10.0.403
.NET 11 previews 11.0.0-rc.3.26522.148 11.0.100-rc.3.26522.148

Download .NET from https://dotnet.microsoft.com/download/dotnet.

Once you have installed the updated runtime or SDK, restart your apps for the update to take effect.

If you have deployed self-contained applications, rebuild and redeploy those applications with the updated runtime.

For NativeAOT applications, update the SDK and any explicit compiler or runtime-pack references to patched versions, then republish and redeploy the application. Updating the machine's shared runtime alone does not replace a decoder already linked into a NativeAOT executable.

Other Information

Reporting Security Issues

If you have found a potential security issue in a supported version of .NET, please report it to the Microsoft Security Response Center (MSRC) via the MSRC Researcher Portal. Further information can be found in the MSRC Report an Issue FAQ.

Security reports made through MSRC may qualify for the Microsoft .NET Bounty. Details of the Microsoft .NET Bounty Program including terms and conditions are at https://aka.ms/corebounty.

Support

You can ask questions about this issue on GitHub in the .NET GitHub organization. The main repos are located at https://github.com/dotnet/runtime. The Announcements repo (https://github.com/dotnet/Announcements) will contain this bulletin as an issue and will include a link to a discussion issue. You can ask questions in the linked discussion issue.

entry.title: [Microsoft.NETCore.App.Runtime.maccatalyst-arm64] Microsoft Security Advisory CVE-2026-111497 - .NET Brotli Decoder Out-of-bounds Write Vulnerability
entry.content:
Executive summary

A buffer overflow vulnerability exists in the Brotli decompression library used by .NET. This vulnerability may allow an unauthenticated attacker to read or corrupt process memory. This could lead to information disclosure, denial of service, or elevation of privilege.

ASP.NET Core and HttpClient do not automatically decompress Brotli data in their default configurations. Applications are exposed when they enable Brotli decompression or explicitly use Brotli decompression APIs to process attacker-controlled data, as described below. .NET Framework is not affected.

Announcement

Announcement for this issue can be found at https://github.com/dotnet/announcements/issues/494

CVSS Details

  • Version: 3.1
  • Severity: High
  • Score: 8.1
  • Vector: CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:H/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H/E:U/RL:O/RC:C
  • Weakness: CWE-787 (Out-of-bounds Write)

Affected Platforms

  • Platforms: All
  • Architectures: All

Mitigations

ASP.NET Core request decompression and HttpClient automatic response decompression are not enabled by default. An application is not exposed merely because an affected .NET package is installed. Exposure requires the application to decompress attacker-controlled Brotli data through one of these paths:

  • Enable ASP.NET Core automatic request decompression with Brotli (br) support.
  • Enable HttpClient automatic response decompression by configuring HttpClientHandler.AutomaticDecompression or SocketsHttpHandler.AutomaticDecompression to include DecompressionMethods.Brotli or DecompressionMethods.All.
  • Explicitly use Brotli decompression APIs in System.IO.Compression, such as BrotliStream or BrotliDecoder.

Until the update can be deployed, avoid decompressing attacker-controlled Brotli data.

The following examples show how to disable Brotli decompression if you are already using it.

Warning: Do not use these code snippets if you are not already using decompression. Do not introduce a call to AddRequestDecompression if your application does not already call it. Similarly, do not introduce an AutomaticDecompression property assignment if your application does not already set that property. Modify only your existing decompression configuration. Enabling automatic decompression can introduce denial-of-service risks even when Brotli is excluded.

If you are already using Brotli request decompression in ASP.NET Core, exclude it by removing the br entry from your existing decompression configuration. This retains the default gzip and deflate providers:

builder.Services.AddRequestDecompression(options =>
{
    options.DecompressionProviders.Remove("br");
});

If your application already enables HttpClient automatic response decompression, disable Brotli by updating the flags on your existing handler so they do not include DecompressionMethods.Brotli:

var handler = new HttpClientHandler
{
    AutomaticDecompression = DecompressionMethods.GZip | DecompressionMethods.Deflate
};

var httpClient = new HttpClient(handler);

Applications that directly use Brotli decompression APIs must stop passing untrusted Brotli data to those APIs until updated. Ensure that other application code does not continue to decompress the same untrusted Brotli data. These changes can affect normal request and response handling and should be tested before deployment. Installing the security update remains the recommended fix.

Affected Packages

The vulnerability affects .NET applications using an affected Brotli decoder in the runtime or NativeAOT packages listed below.

Advisory FAQ

How do I know if I am affected?

You are affected if your application uses an affected Brotli decoder included in a package listed in affected packages, including a decoder linked into a NativeAOT application, to decompress attacker-controlled data. See mitigations for the affected usage paths and default settings.

How do I fix the issue?

Install the updated runtime or SDK for the .NET version used by your application. If your application directly references an affected package, update that reference to the patched version listed above.

.NET release Runtime SDK versions
.NET 8 8.0.33 8.0.133, 8.0.427
.NET 9 9.0.22 9.0.123, 9.0.320
.NET 10 10.0.14 10.0.114, 10.0.403
.NET 11 previews 11.0.0-rc.3.26522.148 11.0.100-rc.3.26522.148

Download .NET from https://dotnet.microsoft.com/download/dotnet.

Once you have installed the updated runtime or SDK, restart your apps for the update to take effect.

If you have deployed self-contained applications, rebuild and redeploy those applications with the updated runtime.

For NativeAOT applications, update the SDK and any explicit compiler or runtime-pack references to patched versions, then republish and redeploy the application. Updating the machine's shared runtime alone does not replace a decoder already linked into a NativeAOT executable.

Other Information

Reporting Security Issues

If you have found a potential security issue in a supported version of .NET, please report it to the Microsoft Security Response Center (MSRC) via the MSRC Researcher Portal. Further information can be found in the MSRC Report an Issue FAQ.

Security reports made through MSRC may qualify for the Microsoft .NET Bounty. Details of the Microsoft .NET Bounty Program including terms and conditions are at https://aka.ms/corebounty.

Support

You can ask questions about this issue on GitHub in the .NET GitHub organization. The main repos are located at https://github.com/dotnet/runtime. The Announcements repo (https://github.com/dotnet/Announcements) will contain this bulletin as an issue and will include a link to a discussion issue. You can ask questions in the linked discussion issue.

entry.title: [Microsoft.NETCore.App.Runtime.linux-x64] Microsoft Security Advisory CVE-2026-111497 - .NET Brotli Decoder Out-of-bounds Write Vulnerability
entry.content:
Executive summary

A buffer overflow vulnerability exists in the Brotli decompression library used by .NET. This vulnerability may allow an unauthenticated attacker to read or corrupt process memory. This could lead to information disclosure, denial of service, or elevation of privilege.

ASP.NET Core and HttpClient do not automatically decompress Brotli data in their default configurations. Applications are exposed when they enable Brotli decompression or explicitly use Brotli decompression APIs to process attacker-controlled data, as described below. .NET Framework is not affected.

Announcement

Announcement for this issue can be found at https://github.com/dotnet/announcements/issues/494

CVSS Details

  • Version: 3.1
  • Severity: High
  • Score: 8.1
  • Vector: CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:H/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H/E:U/RL:O/RC:C
  • Weakness: CWE-787 (Out-of-bounds Write)

Affected Platforms

  • Platforms: All
  • Architectures: All

Mitigations

ASP.NET Core request decompression and HttpClient automatic response decompression are not enabled by default. An application is not exposed merely because an affected .NET package is installed. Exposure requires the application to decompress attacker-controlled Brotli data through one of these paths:

  • Enable ASP.NET Core automatic request decompression with Brotli (br) support.
  • Enable HttpClient automatic response decompression by configuring HttpClientHandler.AutomaticDecompression or SocketsHttpHandler.AutomaticDecompression to include DecompressionMethods.Brotli or DecompressionMethods.All.
  • Explicitly use Brotli decompression APIs in System.IO.Compression, such as BrotliStream or BrotliDecoder.

Until the update can be deployed, avoid decompressing attacker-controlled Brotli data.

The following examples show how to disable Brotli decompression if you are already using it.

Warning: Do not use these code snippets if you are not already using decompression. Do not introduce a call to AddRequestDecompression if your application does not already call it. Similarly, do not introduce an AutomaticDecompression property assignment if your application does not already set that property. Modify only your existing decompression configuration. Enabling automatic decompression can introduce denial-of-service risks even when Brotli is excluded.

If you are already using Brotli request decompression in ASP.NET Core, exclude it by removing the br entry from your existing decompression configuration. This retains the default gzip and deflate providers:

builder.Services.AddRequestDecompression(options =>
{
    options.DecompressionProviders.Remove("br");
});

If your application already enables HttpClient automatic response decompression, disable Brotli by updating the flags on your existing handler so they do not include DecompressionMethods.Brotli:

var handler = new HttpClientHandler
{
    AutomaticDecompression = DecompressionMethods.GZip | DecompressionMethods.Deflate
};

var httpClient = new HttpClient(handler);

Applications that directly use Brotli decompression APIs must stop passing untrusted Brotli data to those APIs until updated. Ensure that other application code does not continue to decompress the same untrusted Brotli data. These changes can affect normal request and response handling and should be tested before deployment. Installing the security update remains the recommended fix.

Affected Packages

The vulnerability affects .NET applications using an affected Brotli decoder in the runtime or NativeAOT packages listed below.

Advisory FAQ

How do I know if I am affected?

You are affected if your application uses an affected Brotli decoder included in a package listed in affected packages, including a decoder linked into a NativeAOT application, to decompress attacker-controlled data. See mitigations for the affected usage paths and default settings.

How do I fix the issue?

Install the updated runtime or SDK for the .NET version used by your application. If your application directly references an affected package, update that reference to the patched version listed above.

.NET release Runtime SDK versions
.NET 8 8.0.33 8.0.133, 8.0.427
.NET 9 9.0.22 9.0.123, 9.0.320
.NET 10 10.0.14 10.0.114, 10.0.403
.NET 11 previews 11.0.0-rc.3.26522.148 11.0.100-rc.3.26522.148

Download .NET from https://dotnet.microsoft.com/download/dotnet.

Once you have installed the updated runtime or SDK, restart your apps for the update to take effect.

If you have deployed self-contained applications, rebuild and redeploy those applications with the updated runtime.

For NativeAOT applications, update the SDK and any explicit compiler or runtime-pack references to patched versions, then republish and redeploy the application. Updating the machine's shared runtime alone does not replace a decoder already linked into a NativeAOT executable.

Other Information

Reporting Security Issues

If you have found a potential security issue in a supported version of .NET, please report it to the Microsoft Security Response Center (MSRC) via the MSRC Researcher Portal. Further information can be found in the MSRC Report an Issue FAQ.

Security reports made through MSRC may qualify for the Microsoft .NET Bounty. Details of the Microsoft .NET Bounty Program including terms and conditions are at https://aka.ms/corebounty.

Support

You can ask questions about this issue on GitHub in the .NET GitHub organization. The main repos are located at https://github.com/dotnet/runtime. The Announcements repo (https://github.com/dotnet/Announcements) will contain this bulletin as an issue and will include a link to a discussion issue. You can ask questions in the linked discussion issue.

entry.title: [Microsoft.NETCore.App.Runtime.linux-musl-x64] Microsoft Security Advisory CVE-2026-111497 - .NET Brotli Decoder Out-of-bounds Write Vulnerability
entry.content:
Executive summary

A buffer overflow vulnerability exists in the Brotli decompression library used by .NET. This vulnerability may allow an unauthenticated attacker to read or corrupt process memory. This could lead to information disclosure, denial of service, or elevation of privilege.

ASP.NET Core and HttpClient do not automatically decompress Brotli data in their default configurations. Applications are exposed when they enable Brotli decompression or explicitly use Brotli decompression APIs to process attacker-controlled data, as described below. .NET Framework is not affected.

Announcement

Announcement for this issue can be found at https://github.com/dotnet/announcements/issues/494

CVSS Details

  • Version: 3.1
  • Severity: High
  • Score: 8.1
  • Vector: CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:H/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H/E:U/RL:O/RC:C
  • Weakness: CWE-787 (Out-of-bounds Write)

Affected Platforms

  • Platforms: All
  • Architectures: All

Mitigations

ASP.NET Core request decompression and HttpClient automatic response decompression are not enabled by default. An application is not exposed merely because an affected .NET package is installed. Exposure requires the application to decompress attacker-controlled Brotli data through one of these paths:

  • Enable ASP.NET Core automatic request decompression with Brotli (br) support.
  • Enable HttpClient automatic response decompression by configuring HttpClientHandler.AutomaticDecompression or SocketsHttpHandler.AutomaticDecompression to include DecompressionMethods.Brotli or DecompressionMethods.All.
  • Explicitly use Brotli decompression APIs in System.IO.Compression, such as BrotliStream or BrotliDecoder.

Until the update can be deployed, avoid decompressing attacker-controlled Brotli data.

The following examples show how to disable Brotli decompression if you are already using it.

Warning: Do not use these code snippets if you are not already using decompression. Do not introduce a call to AddRequestDecompression if your application does not already call it. Similarly, do not introduce an AutomaticDecompression property assignment if your application does not already set that property. Modify only your existing decompression configuration. Enabling automatic decompression can introduce denial-of-service risks even when Brotli is excluded.

If you are already using Brotli request decompression in ASP.NET Core, exclude it by removing the br entry from your existing decompression configuration. This retains the default gzip and deflate providers:

builder.Services.AddRequestDecompression(options =>
{
    options.DecompressionProviders.Remove("br");
});

If your application already enables HttpClient automatic response decompression, disable Brotli by updating the flags on your existing handler so they do not include DecompressionMethods.Brotli:

var handler = new HttpClientHandler
{
    AutomaticDecompression = DecompressionMethods.GZip | DecompressionMethods.Deflate
};

var httpClient = new HttpClient(handler);

Applications that directly use Brotli decompression APIs must stop passing untrusted Brotli data to those APIs until updated. Ensure that other application code does not continue to decompress the same untrusted Brotli data. These changes can affect normal request and response handling and should be tested before deployment. Installing the security update remains the recommended fix.

Affected Packages

The vulnerability affects .NET applications using an affected Brotli decoder in the runtime or NativeAOT packages listed below.

Advisory FAQ

How do I know if I am affected?

You are affected if your application uses an affected Brotli decoder included in a package listed in affected packages, including a decoder linked into a NativeAOT application, to decompress attacker-controlled data. See mitigations for the affected usage paths and default settings.

How do I fix the issue?

Install the updated runtime or SDK for the .NET version used by your application. If your application directly references an affected package, update that reference to the patched version listed above.

.NET release Runtime SDK versions
.NET 8 8.0.33 8.0.133, 8.0.427
.NET 9 9.0.22 9.0.123, 9.0.320
.NET 10 10.0.14 10.0.114, 10.0.403
.NET 11 previews 11.0.0-rc.3.26522.148 11.0.100-rc.3.26522.148

Download .NET from https://dotnet.microsoft.com/download/dotnet.

Once you have installed the updated runtime or SDK, restart your apps for the update to take effect.

If you have deployed self-contained applications, rebuild and redeploy those applications with the updated runtime.

For NativeAOT applications, update the SDK and any explicit compiler or runtime-pack references to patched versions, then republish and redeploy the application. Updating the machine's shared runtime alone does not replace a decoder already linked into a NativeAOT executable.

Other Information

Reporting Security Issues

If you have found a potential security issue in a supported version of .NET, please report it to the Microsoft Security Response Center (MSRC) via the MSRC Researcher Portal. Further information can be found in the MSRC Report an Issue FAQ.

Security reports made through MSRC may qualify for the Microsoft .NET Bounty. Details of the Microsoft .NET Bounty Program including terms and conditions are at https://aka.ms/corebounty.

Support

You can ask questions about this issue on GitHub in the .NET GitHub organization. The main repos are located at https://github.com/dotnet/runtime. The Announcements repo (https://github.com/dotnet/Announcements) will contain this bulletin as an issue and will include a link to a discussion issue. You can ask questions in the linked discussion issue.

entry.title: [Microsoft.NETCore.App.Runtime.linux-musl-arm64] Microsoft Security Advisory CVE-2026-111497 - .NET Brotli Decoder Out-of-bounds Write Vulnerability
entry.content:
Executive summary

A buffer overflow vulnerability exists in the Brotli decompression library used by .NET. This vulnerability may allow an unauthenticated attacker to read or corrupt process memory. This could lead to information disclosure, denial of service, or elevation of privilege.

ASP.NET Core and HttpClient do not automatically decompress Brotli data in their default configurations. Applications are exposed when they enable Brotli decompression or explicitly use Brotli decompression APIs to process attacker-controlled data, as described below. .NET Framework is not affected.

Announcement

Announcement for this issue can be found at https://github.com/dotnet/announcements/issues/494

CVSS Details

  • Version: 3.1
  • Severity: High
  • Score: 8.1
  • Vector: CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:H/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H/E:U/RL:O/RC:C
  • Weakness: CWE-787 (Out-of-bounds Write)

Affected Platforms

  • Platforms: All
  • Architectures: All

Mitigations

ASP.NET Core request decompression and HttpClient automatic response decompression are not enabled by default. An application is not exposed merely because an affected .NET package is installed. Exposure requires the application to decompress attacker-controlled Brotli data through one of these paths:

  • Enable ASP.NET Core automatic request decompression with Brotli (br) support.
  • Enable HttpClient automatic response decompression by configuring HttpClientHandler.AutomaticDecompression or SocketsHttpHandler.AutomaticDecompression to include DecompressionMethods.Brotli or DecompressionMethods.All.
  • Explicitly use Brotli decompression APIs in System.IO.Compression, such as BrotliStream or BrotliDecoder.

Until the update can be deployed, avoid decompressing attacker-controlled Brotli data.

The following examples show how to disable Brotli decompression if you are already using it.

Warning: Do not use these code snippets if you are not already using decompression. Do not introduce a call to AddRequestDecompression if your application does not already call it. Similarly, do not introduce an AutomaticDecompression property assignment if your application does not already set that property. Modify only your existing decompression configuration. Enabling automatic decompression can introduce denial-of-service risks even when Brotli is excluded.

If you are already using Brotli request decompression in ASP.NET Core, exclude it by removing the br entry from your existing decompression configuration. This retains the default gzip and deflate providers:

builder.Services.AddRequestDecompression(options =>
{
    options.DecompressionProviders.Remove("br");
});

If your application already enables HttpClient automatic response decompression, disable Brotli by updating the flags on your existing handler so they do not include DecompressionMethods.Brotli:

var handler = new HttpClientHandler
{
    AutomaticDecompression = DecompressionMethods.GZip | DecompressionMethods.Deflate
};

var httpClient = new HttpClient(handler);

Applications that directly use Brotli decompression APIs must stop passing untrusted Brotli data to those APIs until updated. Ensure that other application code does not continue to decompress the same untrusted Brotli data. These changes can affect normal request and response handling and should be tested before deployment. Installing the security update remains the recommended fix.

Affected Packages

The vulnerability affects .NET applications using an affected Brotli decoder in the runtime or NativeAOT packages listed below.
